questiontext.text: What is the time complexity of a range query (e.g. sum over [l, r]) on a segment tree?

feedback.text: Correct — a query touches O(log n) canonical nodes.
Only a precomputed prefix-sum array gives O(1) sum, but it cannot handle updates cheaply.
That is a naive scan; the tree avoids it.
That is the cost of many queries or a sort, not a single query.

generalfeedback.text: A segment tree decomposes any range into O(log n) nodes, so both range queries and point updates run in O(log n).

questiontext.text: For an array of n elements, what are the typical build time and space of a segment tree?

feedback.text: Correct — a bottom-up build is linear and the node count is O(n).

answer.text: Build O(n log n), space O(n log n)

feedback.text: The plain segment tree builds in O(n) with O(n) space.

answer.text: Build O(log n), space O(log n)

feedback.text: You must at least visit every element to build, so build is O(n).
Far too much; the structure is linear in space.

generalfeedback.text: Building a segment tree is O(n), and it stores about 2n–4n nodes, i.e. O(n) space.

questiontext.text: What does lazy propagation enable in a segment tree?

answer.text: Range updates in O(log n) by deferring pending updates to child nodes

feedback.text: Correct — a whole range is updated by marking nodes and pushing down only when needed.

answer.text: Sorting the underlying array in O(n)

feedback.text: A segment tree does not sort the array.

answer.text: Reducing space from O(n) to O(log n)

feedback.text: Lazy propagation affects update time, not asymptotic space.
Queries remain O(log n); lazy propagation targets range updates.

generalfeedback.text: Without lazy propagation a range update touches O(n) leaves; with it, updates are deferred and pushed down lazily, giving O(log n) range updates.

questiontext.text: Compared with a Fenwick tree (BIT), a segment tree is more general because it can directly support:

answer.text: Any associative range aggregate, such as range minimum or maximum

feedback.text: Correct — segment trees handle min/max/gcd/etc., not just invertible sums.

answer.text: Only prefix sums and nothing else

feedback.text: That is closer to what a Fenwick tree specializes in.
That is a hash table, unrelated to segment trees.
That is a balanced BST task, not a segment tree's role.

generalfeedback.text: A segment tree supports any associative aggregate over a range (sum, min, max, gcd, ...), making it more general than a Fenwick tree.

questiontext.text: Which statements about segment trees are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It is a binary tree whose nodes represent array intervals

feedback.text: Yes — each internal node covers the union of its children's intervals.

answer.text: Range queries and point updates each run in O(log n)

feedback.text: Yes — both operations touch O(log n) nodes.

answer.text: It requires the underlying array to be kept sorted

feedback.text: No — the array is indexed by position, not sorted by value.

answer.text: It can answer range sums but never range minimums

feedback.text: No — it handles min/max just as easily as sum.

generalfeedback.text: A segment tree is an interval binary tree giving O(log n) range queries and updates for any associative aggregate, with no sorting requirement.

questiontext.text: With lazy propagation, a segment tree can apply a range update in O(log n) time.

feedback.text: Correct — pending updates are deferred and pushed down, so range updates are O(log n).
Lazy propagation does give O(log n) range updates.

questiontext.text: A segment tree can only compute range sums and cannot support range minimum or maximum queries.

feedback.text: No — a segment tree supports any associative aggregate, including min and max.
Correct — sum, min, max, gcd, and other associative aggregates all work.

questiontext.text: The technique that defers pending range updates to child nodes, enabling O(log n) range updates, is called lazy ______.

feedback.text: Correct — lazy propagation.
Correct.
